title: Knowing where you stand
description: You have lost track of where you are in the filesystem. Print the absolute path of the current directory on a line by itself, and nothing else.
objective: Practise printing the current working directory.
setup: mkdir projects
check:
out=$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")
if [ "$out" != "$(pwd)" ] && [ "$out" != "$(pwd -P)" ]; then
  echo "Expected the absolute path of the current directory, alone on one line. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Three empty files at once
description: The current directory is empty. Create three empty files named notes.txt, todo.txt and ideas.txt, all with a single command.
objective: Practise creating empty files, several in one go.
check:
for f in notes.txt todo.txt ideas.txt; do
  if [ ! -f "$f" ]; then
    echo "There is no file named $f."
    exit 1
  fi
  if [ -s "$f" ]; then
    echo "$f should be empty, but it has content."
    exit 1
  fi
done

title: Laying out a project
description: The current directory is empty. Create three directories side by side in it, named src, docs and tests, using one command.
objective: Practise creating several directories with a single command.
check:
for d in src docs tests; do
  if [ ! -d "$d" ]; then
    echo "There is no directory named $d."
    exit 1
  fi
done

title: Seeing the hidden entries too
description: Some entries here have names starting with a dot, and a plain listing leaves those out. Print the name of every entry in the current directory, the hidden ones included, one name per line. The two entries that stand for the directory itself and its parent may appear or not; nothing else may.
objective: Practise listing a directory including its hidden entries.
setup:
printf 'SECRET=1\n' > .env
printf 'build/\n' > .gitignore
printf 'hello\n' > notes.txt
mkdir src
check:
expected=$(printf '%s\n' .env .gitignore notes.txt src)
actual=$(grep -vxE '\.|\.\.' "$CMM_STDOUT" | sort)
if [ "$actual" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected these four names, hidden ones included, one per line:"
  printf '%s\n' "$expected"
  exit 1
fi

title: Jumping back where you came from
description: Change into logs/archive, and then return to the directory you started in by using the shell's shortcut for "the directory I was in before" rather than spelling out a path. Finish by having the absolute path of where you end up printed on the last line of output; the shortcut prints it on its own, so no separate step is needed.
objective: Practise switching back to the previous working directory.
setup: mkdir -p logs/archive
check:
out=$(tail -n 1 "$CMM_STDOUT")
if [ "$out" != "$(pwd)" ] && [ "$out" != "$(pwd -P)" ]; then
  echo "The last line of output should be the absolute path of the starting directory. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Reading with line numbers
description: Print the contents of poem.txt with each line preceded by its line number, counting from 1.
objective: Practise printing a file with its lines numbered.
setup:
printf 'roses are red
violets are blue
shells are fun
' > poem.txt
check:
expected=$(printf '1 roses are red\n2 violets are blue\n3 shells are fun')
actual=$(sed -E 's/^ *([0-9]+)[:[:space:]]+/\1 /' "$CMM_STDOUT")
if [ "$actual" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected every line of poem.txt, each preceded by its number (1, 2, 3). Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Stitching two files together
description: Create full.txt holding the contents of part1.txt followed by the contents of part2.txt. Leave both parts exactly as they are.
objective: Practise joining files one after another into a new file.
setup:
printf 'chapter one\n' > part1.txt
printf 'chapter two\n' > part2.txt
check:
if [ ! -f full.txt ]; then
  echo "There is no full.txt."
  exit 1
fi
if [ "$(cat full.txt)" != "$(printf 'chapter one\nchapter two')" ]; then
  echo "full.txt should hold part1.txt then part2.txt. It reads:"
  cat full.txt
  exit 1
fi
if [ "$(cat part1.txt)" != "chapter one" ] || [ "$(cat part2.txt)" != "chapter two" ]; then
  echo "part1.txt and part2.txt must be left unchanged."
  exit 1
fi

title: A name that lies
description: funny.gif claims by its name to be an image. Without opening it, ask the system to inspect its contents and report what kind of data it really holds. The report should name the file and its real type.
objective: Practise identifying a file's type from its contents rather than its name.
setup: printf 'just a note, not a picture\n' > funny.gif
check:
if ! grep -q 'funny.gif' "$CMM_STDOUT" || ! grep -qi 'text' "$CMM_STDOUT"; then
  echo "Expected a report naming funny.gif and saying what it really contains (it is plain text). Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Leaving with a message
description: End the shell so that whatever started it is told the run finished with status 3.
objective: Practise leaving the shell with a chosen exit status.
check:
if [ "$CMM_EXIT" != "3" ]; then
  echo "The shell should have ended with status 3, but it ended with $CMM_EXIT."
  exit 1
fi

title: Asking the shell about itself
description: The command that changes directory is built into the shell itself, so it has no separate program on disk. Print the shell's own built-in documentation for it: its usage line followed by its description.
objective: Practise reading the shell's built-in help for one of its builtins.
check:
if ! grep -q '^cd: cd' "$CMM_STDOUT" || ! grep -qi 'directory' "$CMM_STDOUT"; then
  echo "Expected the shell's own help text for its directory-changing builtin, starting with its usage line. Got:"
  head -n 5 "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Naming a shortcut
description: Define a shortcut named ll that the shell will replace with the text ls -l. Then, in the same command line, ask the shell to print how it has stored that one shortcut.
objective: Practise defining an alias and inspecting its definition.
check:
if ! grep -qxF "alias ll='ls -l'" "$CMM_STDOUT"; then
  echo "Expected the shell to print the stored definition of ll, standing for ls -l. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Climbing back up
description: Change into src/app/lib. From there, move up two levels, and print the absolute path of the directory you end up in.
objective: Practise moving to parent directories with relative paths.
setup: mkdir -p src/app/lib
check:
out=$(tail -n 1 "$CMM_STDOUT")
if [ "$out" != "$(pwd)/src" ] && [ "$out" != "$(pwd -P)/src" ]; then
  echo "Two levels up from src/app/lib is src. Expected its absolute path on the last line. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Biggest first
description: Print the names of the files in the current directory ordered from the largest to the smallest, one name per line and nothing else.
objective: Practise listing a directory sorted by file size.
setup:
printf 'tiny\n' > a-small.txt
printf '%3000s\n' '' > b-huge.log
printf '%1500s\n' '' > c-medium.csv
check:
expected=$(printf '%s\n' b-huge.log c-medium.csv a-small.txt)
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected the names ordered largest to smallest:"
  printf '%s\n' "$expected"
  exit 1
fi

title: Copying a whole family of files
description: Copy every file whose name ends in .txt into backup/ with a single command that does not name the files one by one. The originals must stay where they are, and nothing else may end up in backup/.
objective: Practise copying several files at once with a name pattern.
setup:
printf 'january\n' > jan.txt
printf 'february\n' > feb.txt
printf 'read me\n' > readme.md
mkdir backup
check:
expected=$(printf '%s\n' feb.txt jan.txt)
actual=$(ls backup | sort)
if [ "$actual" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "backup/ should hold exactly feb.txt and jan.txt. It holds:"
  ls backup
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f jan.txt ] || [ ! -f feb.txt ]; then
  echo "The original .txt files must stay where they were."
  exit 1
fi
if ! cmp -s jan.txt backup/jan.txt || ! cmp -s feb.txt backup/feb.txt; then
  echo "The copies in backup/ should match the originals."
  exit 1
fi

title: Tidying the photos
description: Move every file whose name ends in .jpg into photos/ with a single command that does not name the files one by one. Nothing else may move.
objective: Practise moving several files into a directory at once.
setup:
printf 'sand\n' > beach.jpg
printf 'lights\n' > city.jpg
printf 'brand\n' > logo.png
mkdir photos
check:
expected=$(printf '%s\n' beach.jpg city.jpg)
actual=$(ls photos | sort)
if [ "$actual" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "photos/ should hold exactly beach.jpg and city.jpg. It holds:"
  ls photos
  exit 1
fi
if [ -e beach.jpg ] || [ -e city.jpg ]; then
  echo "The .jpg files should have moved, not been copied: they are still in the current directory."
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f logo.png ]; then
  echo "logo.png should have stayed where it was."
  exit 1
fi

title: Clearing out the leftovers
description: Delete every file in the current directory whose name ends in .tmp, with a single command that does not name them one by one. Every other file must survive.
objective: Practise removing files that match a name pattern.
setup:
printf 'x\n' > cache.tmp
printf 'x\n' > session.tmp
printf 'numbers\n' > report.txt
printf 'ideas\n' > draft.md
check:
if [ -e cache.tmp ] || [ -e session.tmp ]; then
  echo "Some .tmp files are still there:"
  ls *.tmp 2>/dev/null || true
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f report.txt ] || [ ! -f draft.md ]; then
  echo "Only the .tmp files should be gone; report.txt and draft.md must survive."
  exit 1
fi

title: Throwing away the build
description: Delete the build directory and everything inside it. It is not empty, and removing a directory together with its contents has to be asked for explicitly, or the command refuses. Leave src alone.
objective: Practise removing a whole directory tree.
setup:
mkdir -p build/obj src
printf 'bin\n' > build/app
printf 'obj\n' > build/obj/main.o
printf 'int main(){}\n' > src/main.c
check:
if [ -e build ]; then
  echo "build is still there."
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f src/main.c ]; then
  echo "src and its contents must be left alone."
  exit 1
fi

title: Mapping the directory tree
description: Print the path of every directory below the current one, at any depth, and no files. Paths may come out in any order and may be written with or without a leading "./". The current directory itself may be listed or not.
objective: Practise searching a tree for entries of one type.
setup:
mkdir -p docs/img src/app/lib
printf 'hi\n' > docs/readme.md
printf 'png\n' > docs/img/logo.png
printf 'code\n' > src/app/lib/util.c
printf 'top\n' > notes.txt
check:
expected=$(printf '%s\n' docs docs/img src src/app src/app/lib)
actual=$(sed 's|^\./||; s|/$||' "$CMM_STDOUT" | grep -vxE '\.?' | sort)
if [ "$actual" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected exactly these directories, and no files:"
  printf '%s\n' "$expected"
  exit 1
fi

title: Builtin or program?
description: Find out what kind of command cd and ls each are: whether the shell carries it out itself or runs a program from disk. Print the shell's answer for both, in one command.
objective: Practise asking the shell what kind of command a name refers to.
check:
long_ok=false
if grep -q '^cd is a shell builtin' "$CMM_STDOUT" && grep -Eq '^ls is ' "$CMM_STDOUT"; then
  long_ok=true
fi
short_ok=false
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" = "$(printf 'builtin\nfile')" ]; then
  short_ok=true
fi
if [ "$long_ok" != true ] && [ "$short_ok" != true ]; then
  echo "Expected the shell to say that cd is a builtin and what ls is. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Just the type, please
description: Report the MIME type of funny.gif, judged from its contents rather than its name. Print only the type itself, in the form image/png, with no file name in front of it.
objective: Practise asking for a file's MIME type in a bare form.
setup: printf 'just a note, not a picture\n' > funny.gif
check:
out=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$CMM_STDOUT")
if [ "$out" != "text/plain" ]; then
  echo "Expected only the MIME type, which is text/plain, with nothing in front of it. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Borrowing a timestamp
description: copy.txt has to carry exactly the same modification time as original.txt. Take the time straight from original.txt rather than typing a date in. Leave the contents of both files, and original.txt's time, alone.
objective: Practise setting a file's timestamp from a reference file.
setup:
printf 'v1\n' > original.txt
printf 'v1\n' > copy.txt
touch -t 202001011200 original.txt
touch -t 202405051200 copy.txt
check:
touch -t 202001011201 .cmm-ref
if ! [ original.txt -ot .cmm-ref ]; then
  rm -f .cmm-ref
  echo "original.txt's modification time changed; only copy.txt should change."
  exit 1
fi
rm -f .cmm-ref
if [ copy.txt -nt original.txt ] || [ copy.txt -ot original.txt ]; then
  echo "copy.txt and original.txt still have different modification times."
  exit 1
fi

title: A copy that remembers when
description: Copy report.txt into archive/ so that the copy keeps the original's modification time. Copying normally stamps the new file with the moment it was made; keeping the original's attributes has to be asked for.
objective: Practise copying a file while preserving its attributes.
setup:
printf 'q4 numbers\n' > report.txt
touch -t 202001011200 report.txt
mkdir archive
check:
if [ ! -f archive/report.txt ]; then
  echo "There is no archive/report.txt."
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f report.txt ]; then
  echo "report.txt should have been copied, not moved."
  exit 1
fi
if ! cmp -s report.txt archive/report.txt; then
  echo "archive/report.txt should match report.txt."
  exit 1
fi
if [ archive/report.txt -nt report.txt ] || [ archive/report.txt -ot report.txt ]; then
  echo "The copy got a new modification time instead of keeping the original's."
  exit 1
fi

title: Moving without trampling
description: Move draft.txt and summary.txt into final/ with one command. final/ already holds an approved draft.txt that must not be replaced: moving normally overwrites a file of the same name without a word, so the command has to be told to leave existing files alone. The local draft.txt may simply stay where it is.
objective: Practise moving files without overwriting existing ones.
setup:
printf 'rough\n' > draft.txt
printf 'short\n' > summary.txt
mkdir final
printf 'approved\n' > final/draft.txt
check:
if [ "$(cat final/draft.txt)" != "approved" ]; then
  echo "final/draft.txt was overwritten; the approved version is gone."
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f final/summary.txt ] || [ -e summary.txt ]; then
  echo "summary.txt should have moved into final/."
  exit 1
fi

title: A directory for your eyes only
description: Create a directory named secret that only its owner can read, write or enter, with no access at all for the group or anyone else. Set those permissions as part of creating it.
objective: Practise creating a directory with specific permissions.
check:
if [ ! -d secret ]; then
  echo "There is no directory named secret."
  exit 1
fi
perms=$(ls -ld secret | cut -c1-10)
if [ "$perms" != "drwx------" ]; then
  echo "secret should be drwx------ (owner only), but it is $perms."
  exit 1
fi

title: A shortcut that survives
description: Make a shortcut named ll, standing for ls -l, permanent: record it in the startup file that interactive Bash shells read from your home directory, so every new shell has it. Keep whatever that file already contains.
objective: Practise persisting an alias in the shell's startup file.
setup: printf 'export EDITOR=vi\n' > .bashrc
check:
if ! grep -q 'export EDITOR=vi' "$HOME/.bashrc"; then
  echo "The startup file lost what it already contained."
  exit 1
fi
out=$(bash -c 'shopt -s expand_aliases; . "$HOME/.bashrc"; alias ll' 2>/dev/null || true)
if [ "$out" != "alias ll='ls -l'" ]; then
  echo "A new shell reading the startup file does not get ll as a shortcut for ls -l."
  exit 1
fi

title: Seeing through the link
description: current is a symbolic link to the release directory in use. Change into it and print the absolute path of where you really are, with the link resolved: the real directory's path, not the path through current.
objective: Practise printing the physical working directory, symlinks resolved.
setup:
mkdir -p releases/v2
ln -s releases/v2 current
check:
out=$(tail -n 1 "$CMM_STDOUT")
if [ "$out" != "$(pwd -P)/releases/v2" ]; then
  echo "Expected the real absolute path, $(pwd -P)/releases/v2. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: The detailed, oldest-first listing
description: Print a detailed listing of the current directory, one line per file showing its permissions, owner, size and modification time. Sizes must be shown in human-friendly units such as 2.0K rather than raw byte counts, and the files must be ordered by modification time, with the oldest first and the most recently changed last.
objective: Practise combining listing options: long format, readable sizes, and reverse time order.
setup:
printf '%2047s\n' '' > report.pdf
printf '%5119s\n' '' > notes.txt
printf '%3071s\n' '' > photo.jpg
touch -t 202301011200 report.pdf
touch -t 202302011200 notes.txt
touch -t 202303011200 photo.jpg
check:
lines=$(grep '^-' "$CMM_STDOUT" || true)
if [ -z "$lines" ]; then
  echo "Expected a detailed listing, one line per file with permissions, owner, size and time."
  exit 1
fi
names=$(printf '%s\n' "$lines" | awk '{print $NF}')
expected=$(printf '%s\n' report.pdf notes.txt photo.jpg)
if [ "$names" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected the files oldest first, newest last:"
  printf '%s\n' "$expected"
  exit 1
fi
if printf '%s\n' "$lines" | awk '{print $5}' | grep -vqE '^[0-9.]+K$'; then
  echo "Sizes should be human-friendly, such as 2.0K, not raw byte counts."
  exit 1
fi

title: The other printf
description: printf is both a shell command and a C library function, and each has its own manual page in a different section. Print the manual page for the C library function, the one in section 3, not the shell command's page.
objective: Practise opening a manual page from a specific section.
check:
text=$(sed $'s/.\b//g' "$CMM_STDOUT")
if ! printf '%s\n' "$text" | head -n 5 | grep -qi 'printf(3)'; then
  echo "Expected the section 3 manual page for printf, whose header reads PRINTF(3). Got:"
  printf '%s\n' "$text" | head -n 3
  exit 1
fi

title: Where does printf live?
description: Print the one-line summaries the manual database holds for pages named printf, so you can see which manual sections it appears in. Only the one-line summaries, not a full manual page.
objective: Practise looking up short manual descriptions and their section numbers.
check:
norm=$(sed 's/ *(/(/g' "$CMM_STDOUT")
if ! printf '%s\n' "$norm" | grep -q 'printf(1)' || ! printf '%s\n' "$norm" | grep -q 'printf(3)'; then
  echo "Expected one-line summaries showing printf in sections 1 and 3. Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi
if [ "$(wc -l < "$CMM_STDOUT")" -gt 40 ]; then
  echo "That is a full manual page; only the one-line summaries were asked for."
  exit 1
fi

title: Finding the heavy files
description: Print the path of every regular file anywhere below the current directory that is larger than 100 bytes. Directories must not appear, however large they are. Paths may come out in any order and may be written with or without a leading "./".
objective: Practise searching a tree by file type and size.
setup:
mkdir -p logs data
printf '%299s\n' '' > logs/big.log
printf '%249s\n' '' > data/huge.csv
printf '%49s\n' '' > data/small.csv
printf 'hi\n' > notes.txt
check:
expected=$(printf '%s\n' data/huge.csv logs/big.log)
actual=$(sed 's|^\./||' "$CMM_STDOUT" | sort)
if [ "$actual" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected exactly these files over 100 bytes:"
  printf '%s\n' "$expected"
  exit 1
fi

title: Sweeping out the backups
description: Delete every file whose name ends in .bak, wherever it sits below the current directory and however deep, with one command. Every other file must survive.
objective: Practise searching a tree and acting on every match.
setup:
mkdir -p a/b
printf 'x\n' > top.bak
printf 'x\n' > a/mid.bak
printf 'x\n' > a/b/deep.bak
printf 'keep\n' > keep.txt
printf 'keep\n' > a/b/notes.txt
check:
left=$(find . -name '*.bak')
if [ -n "$left" ]; then
  echo "Some .bak files are still there:"
  printf '%s\n' "$left"
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f keep.txt ] || [ ! -f a/b/notes.txt ]; then
  echo "Only the .bak files should be gone; keep.txt and a/b/notes.txt must survive."
  exit 1
fi

title: Adding one file onto another
description: Add the contents of more.txt to the end of notes.txt. The lines already in notes.txt must survive (the obvious way of sending output into a file empties it first, and this must not), and more.txt must stay as it is.
objective: Practise appending a file's contents to another file.
setup:
printf 'line one
line two
' > notes.txt
printf 'line three
' > more.txt
check:
if [ "$(cat notes.txt)" = "line three" ]; then
  echo "notes.txt now holds only more.txt's line: its original content was overwritten instead of added to."
  exit 1
fi
if [ "$(cat notes.txt)" != "$(printf 'line one\nline two\nline three')" ]; then
  echo "notes.txt should read line one, line two, line three. It reads:"
  cat notes.txt
  exit 1
fi
if [ "$(cat more.txt)" != "line three" ]; then
  echo "more.txt must be left unchanged."
  exit 1
fi
